# Migri Processing Times 2026 — Current Waits by Permit Type, Statutory Maximums and What to Do About a Delay

Migri processing times by permit type, checked 14 October 2026: work, specialist, Fast Track, student and family. When the clock starts and what to do about a delay.

Written by · Erkan Bayar Legal review · Samed Karakas, Legal Counsel Sources checked · 2026-10-14 Reading time · 13 min

## Short answer

Checked against Migri on 14 October 2026: first permits for employed persons (TTOL) that ended in a positive decision took an average of 17 days in July 2026, specialists usually get a decision in about two weeks, and Fast Track for specialists, EU Blue Card holders and start-up entrepreneurs has a 14-day target. About 82% of positive decisions on first student permits come within 30 days. Family-based applications have a statutory maximum of nine months, and Migri has reported backlogs in them. The clock starts when you prove your identity, not when you submit, and the card takes about two more weeks after the decision. Migri publishes two estimates per application type — most cases and a minority of cases — and if yours has not been taken up within the shorter one, the longer applies. Statutory maximums are a separate thing: two months for work-based permits, three for studies and nine for family ties. If you applied for an extension before the old permit expired, you may keep working while you wait. Migri asks you not to call when an estimate is exceeded; if a statutory maximum is exceeded, a free complaint to the Parliamentary Ombudsman is possible, but the Ombudsman cannot change a decision.

## The tool for this

- Migri fees 2026: what each application costs The fee for this application, online and on paper, and when it is not refunded.
- Which documents do you need? The checklist for this application, with what has to be translated or legalised.

## 1. Current Migri processing times by permit type

The table collects what Migri itself was reporting when we checked on 14 October 2026, next to the time limit set by law or by Migri's own service target. Migri states its figures in different forms for different permits — an average for one, a most-cases estimate for another, the share decided within a month for a third — and the table keeps each figure in the form Migri used rather than turning them into a single number Migri never published.

None of these is a promise for your application. Migri updates its estimates every two months and the averages for employed persons every month, so before you fix a start date or book a flight, open Migri's processing-times page or its processing-time checker, choose your exact application type and read the current figure there. Where we could not verify a current figure from Migri for a permit type, the table says so instead of guessing.

| Application | What Migri reports | Limit in law or service target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Employed person (TTOL), first permit | Most cases one month, a minority two months; positive decisions averaged 17 days in July 2026 | Two months in law, counted from the biometrics visit; Migri's own goal is one month |
| Employed person (TTOL), extended permit | Averages for July 2026: 37 days for positive decisions, 162 days for refusals | Two months in law |
| Specialist | About two weeks in most cases, up to two months in a minority | Two months in law; Fast Track target 14 days for a first permit |
| EU Blue Card | First permits can go through Fast Track; for extensions, read the live estimate | Two months in law; Fast Track target 14 days for a first permit |
| Start-up entrepreneur | Can go through Fast Track once Business Finland has issued its statement | Fast Track target 14 days |
| Studies, first permit | About 82% of positive decisions within 30 days; with no decision by then, Migri's estimate is 90 days | Three months in law |
| Family ties, first permit | Migri has reported backlogs; read the live estimate for your exact family category | Nine months in law; 90 days for a student's family member when no additional information is needed |
| Permanent residence permit | No figure verified; read the live estimate. The requirements changed on 8 January 2026 | No general maximum in law; six months for the EU long-term resident's permit |
| Finnish citizenship | Migri has reported a backlog that it is clearing; read the live estimate | No general maximum in law; 12 months for persons under protection |
| EU citizen, registration of right of residence | Listed under EU citizens in Migri's table; read the live estimate | Six months for the residence card of an EU citizen's family member |

## 2. When the clock starts and when it stops

The most common misunderstanding is that the clock starts the moment you submit. According to Migri the processing time starts when you have proved your identity, which happens at a service point visit or, for some online applications, on submission in Enter Finland. The time ends when the decision is ready.

The card has to be counted in as well. After the decision, producing and posting the residence permit card takes about two more weeks. "The decision is out" and "the card is in my hand" are therefore not the same day, and travel or a starting date at work should be planned around the card.

For work-based permits the Aliens Act says this in so many words: the decision is due within two months of the authority receiving a properly completed application with its attachments, and the time is counted from the visit at which you give your fingerprints and other biometrics — at a Finnish mission or an external service provider abroad, or at a Migri service point in Finland. Migri also says it can start on an employed person's application before identity has been proved, and that an employer who submits the terms of employment without delay speeds the processing up.

## 3. Two estimates and how to read them

For each application type Migri publishes not one time but two estimates: the processing time in most cases and the processing time in a minority of cases. The rule is plain: if your application has not been taken up during the shorter estimate, the longer estimate in the table is the one that applies in your case.

The estimates are based on how long most decisions took in the preceding months and how many similar applications arrived in the past two months; they are updated every two months. The time spent in the queue is included in the estimate. If no additional information has to be requested, the shorter estimate will most likely apply.

For one application rather than a whole permit type, Migri's processing-time checker is the more precise tool. It is built on the same statistics, so it will not move your application forward, but it is the quickest way to see the estimate that applies to your own case rather than to the average applicant.

## 4. Maximum times laid down by law

Alongside the estimate there is also a maximum time laid down by law, and the two should not be confused. The estimate is a statistic; the statutory time is an obligation. Migri's tables show separately which applications have a maximum time provided by law, and not every application has one.

### Checklist

- Residence permits on the basis of work: 2 months, counted from the visit at which biometrics are given
- Residence permit on the basis of studies: 3 months
- Residence permit on the basis of family ties: 9 months
- A student's family member: 90 days from a complete application
- Residence card of an EU citizen's family member: 6 months
- EU long-term resident's residence permit: 6 months
- Citizenship application of persons under protection: 12 months
- Asylum: 18 months where the investigation requires it, and 21 months where the situation in the country of departure is unstable

## 5. Why applications are delayed

Migri lists the reasons for delay on its own page: the number of requirements that have to be investigated, the number of applications arriving for the same permit type, whether automation can be used, and the maximum times prescribed by law. The time spent waiting in the queue belongs to this picture too.

The single most common cause is a request for additional information. If a piece of information or an attachment is missing, Migri asks you for the document and the processing waits for it to arrive. Being invited to an interview, an unpaid processing fee, a requirement that is not met, or a request for an exception all lengthen the time as well. If your application is waiting for information from another authority — an interview at a Finnish mission, for example — Migri cannot influence that authority's waiting times.

## 6. The right to work while you wait

For an employee waiting on an extension there is one decisive date. If you applied for the extended permit before your current permit expired, you may go on working in accordance with that permit while the decision is awaited. If you applied only after the previous permit had expired, you are not allowed to continue working on the basis of the old permit.

There are exceptions. In seasonal work, continuing depends on your going on working for the same employer; with au pair, working holiday and intra-corporate transfer (ICT) permits the right to work ends when the permit ends. An employer may ask the employee to show the residence permit card and a document about the pending application; that document is Migri's certificate of a pending application.

## 7. Migri asks you not to call — so what does help

Migri's wording is plain: you do not need to contact it if the estimate has been exceeded. An automated message is sent when the processing situation of your application changes, an online applicant sees the status in their Enter Finland account, and Migri will contact you if it needs additional information. Customer service cannot give exact details about the processing of your application.

What actually helps is removing in advance the reasons that lengthen the time: applying when you already meet the requirements, applying online through Enter Finland, filling in every section of the form carefully and adding all the required attachments, and paying the processing fee in Enter Finland before you submit. Once these are in order Migri can usually use automation, and the decision comes faster.

There is one formal right alongside Migri's request. Under section 23 of the Administrative Procedure Act (hallintolaki) a matter must be dealt with without undue delay, and the authority must, if the party asks, give an estimate of when the decision will be issued and answer enquiries about how the processing is progressing. When you have a concrete reason — a job with a start date, a lease, a family event — a short written request that cites that section is a legitimate way to get an answer, and far more useful than calling the helpline again.

## 8. When a statutory time is exceeded: complaint options

Exceeding the estimate and exceeding the statutory maximum do not weigh the same. Where the second has happened, a complaint can be made to the Parliamentary Ombudsman (eduskunnan oikeusasiamies). Undue delay in dealing with a matter is expressly among the things the Ombudsman investigates; the complaint is free, and a person may complain on their own, together with others, or on someone else's behalf.

The limits are worth knowing too. The Ombudsman cannot amend or overturn decisions made by authorities; to obtain a change, the legal means of appeal provided by law must be used. As a rule the Ombudsman does not investigate a matter pending before another authority, but delay in the processing is the exception to that rule. A complaint concerning a matter older than two years is not investigated unless there are special reasons.

sources.title: Permit processing time reduces by half — automation speeds up decisions -             Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment
highlights:
The development measures of the employment and economic development services (TE services), the Finnish Immigration Service and the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment reduced the processing time of residence permits for employed persons to an average of 41 days in February 2024 from the previous year’s figure of 77 days.

A faster processing time for favourable decisions is particularly significant. In February 2024, the average processing time was 23 days for first permits and 21 days for extended permits. “The Finnish Immigration Service and TE Offices have done excellent work. We aim to ensure that permit applicants and employers can rely on the promise of a one-month maximum processing time, as outlined in the Government Programme. At the core of this work will continue to be ensuring that abuses are prevented throughout the permit procedure,” says Minister of Employment Arto Satonen. 

In February 2024, TE Offices made a favourable partial decision on first and extended permits in 12 days on average. The Finnish Immigration Service then took, on average, 9 days to make a favourable decision. In February 2023, favourable partial decisions were processed in 44 days and the total processing time was 66 days.

Permit processing time reduces by half — automation speeds up decisions - Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment 

# Joint press release of the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment, the Finnish Immigration Service and TE Offices Permit processing time reduces by half — automation speeds up decisions

 Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment 

 Publication date 25.3.2024 9.18 | Published in English on 25.3.2024 at 10.07 

The development measures of the employment and economic development services (TE services), the Finnish Immigration Service and the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment reduced the processing time of residence permits for employed persons to an average of 41 days in February 2024 from the previous year’s figure of 77 days.

A faster processing time for favourable decisions is particularly significant. In February 2024, the average processing time was 23 days for first permits and 21 days for extended permits. “The Finnish Immigration Service and TE Offices have done excellent work. We aim to ensure that permit applicants and employers can rely on the promise of a one-month maximum processing time, as outlined in the Government Programme. At the core of this work will continue to be ensuring that abuses are prevented throughout the permit procedure,” says Minister of Employment Arto Satonen. 

In February 2024, TE Offices made a favourable partial decision on first and extended permits in 12 days on average. The Finnish Immigration Service then took, on average, 9 days to make a favourable decision. In February 2023, favourable partial decisions were processed in 44 days and the total processing time was 66 days.

“I am particularly proud that the specialists at TE Offices have been closely involved in designing an automation system suitable for partial decisions. This has played a key role in reducing processing times. Together we are committed to developing our processes so that we can offer faster and higher-quality services to both jobseekers and employers,” says Director of Uusimaa TE Office Minna Helenius.

“We are aiming for efficient and controlled permit processes. We will process permits faster than before, while at the same time ensuring effective prevention of abuses through good cooperation between the authorities. We have our staff to thank for the good result and for their excellent work,” says Director General Ilkka Haahtela from the Finnish Immigration Service. 

## Automation speeds up and harmonises processing

Not only have the processing times been significantly reduced, but the waiting lists of applications at TE Offices have also become markedly shorter. In early January 2024, the number of applications awaiting processing exceeded 1,100, but their number had dropped to 59 in February.

In recent years, the Finnish Immigration Service has heavily invested in developing partial automation in decision-making. Decision-making has also been significantly accelerated with the introduction of assistive automation in TE services in January 2024. Automation checks official registers for data that previously had to be manually verified for each application. This saves time, reduces the risk of human error and helps authorities to identify cases involving risks. 

Close cooperation between the authorities, improvements in information exchange and harmonisation of practices have played a key role in accelerating, and improving the quality of, processing. 

Inquiries: Essi Lojander, Senior Specialist, Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment, tel. +358 295 047 313 (from 27 March onwards) Katri Niskanen, Chief Specialist, Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment, tel. +358 295 047 373 (from 25 to 26 March) Veera Svahn, Special Adviser to the Minister of Employment, tel. +358 295 047 321 (questions for the Minister of Employment) Assi Puistolahti, Service Supervisor, Uusimaa Employment and Economic Development Office, tel. +358 295 042 461 Tuuli Huhtilainen, Head of Section, Finnish Immigration Service, tel. +358 295 433436

sources.title: Silvia Nguyen: My Residence Permit in Finland is Valid From Today
highlights:
### How I applied on enterfinland.fi

I hit "submit" the application and paid application fee on May 8th. I created an account with just my email address long before that and drafted my application. The site autosaves every time you fill in something new.

The next period waiting for an appointment to prove our identity at the embassy felt really really long. Since nothing was certain, we didn't buy stuff. But we learned a lot of Finnish together. Facebook groups were full of posts asking if anyone received a decision. Such anxious time. Near the end of June I gave up on expecting the email and thought "ugh whatever" then it came.

On June 23rd, we went to the embassy with all the documents submitted online and scanned our fingerprints.

Just five days later, my hubby's application was approved. Two weeks later, his card arrived and my application was approved. It took my card another two weeks to arrive.

So our application process was nearly three months in total. Although my husband received his decision a few weeks before me, we still can fly together. Mahtava!

If your family submit applications all on the same day, it's likely you two can get the cards in time to go on the same flight.

highlights:
You can receive a residence permit for studies if

...

- you participate in an exchange programme between educational institutions or some other exchange programme. For more information on exchange programmes, please contact your educational institution.

Apply for a residence permit for studies in the Enter Finland online service. Fill in the application carefully and add all the necessary attachments. Make sure that any attachments have been translated into Finnish, Swedish or English.

If your family members are applying with you, make sure that 

- documents related to the family relationship have been legalised
- all the attachments have been translated into Finnish, Swedish or English
- the applications contain the necessary reports on adequate financial resources.

## Book an appointment to prove your identity

Once you have submitted your application in Enter Finland, book an appointment for identification, i.e., to prove your identity. Book the appointment as soon as possible because embassies or consulates may be busy during the summer when many students are applying for their first residence permit. Check the Ministry for Foreign Affairs’ website Finland abroad (finlandabroad.fi), to see which embassy you should visit to prove your identity.

...

At the moment, approximately 75% of those applying for the first residence permit for studies receive a decision within 30 days. 

We aim to process the family members’ applications at the same time as the student’s application if the family members have visited to prove their identity at the same time as the student and their applications contain all the necessary information and attachments. We process family members’ applications within 90 days of submitting a fully completed application. A fully completed application means that the application has been duly filled in and contains all the necessary attachments. Documents related to family relationships must also be legalised.

sources.title: Moving to and Living in Helsinki 2026 | ENB Consulting
highlights:
## Short answer

When relocating to Helsinki, the order of formalities matters: immigration status → DVV/personal identity code/municipality of residence → Vero → Kela → banking/strong authentication → housing/utilities → local services. International House Helsinki / Helsinki-info provides local guidance for international newcomers. A city guide does not replace permit or benefit rules; always verify personal eligibility with Migri, DVV, Vero and Kela.

...

Non-EU nationals should confirm the correct residence permit; EU citizens should check whether registration of the right of residence is required for stays over three months.

...

Common early bottlenecks include civil-status documents, legalisation/translation, DVV appointments, housing and bank KYC. Check marriage/birth-certificate requirements before arrival.

...

Municipality-of-residence registration matters for local public services; having a Finnish personal identity code does not always mean that a municipality of residence has been registered. Kela eligibility is also not automatic merely from an address registration.

Do not delay the tax card when starting work. Strong electronic identification makes access to many public and private services easier.

### Checklist

- Confirm residence permit / EU registration status
- Complete DVV personal identity code and municipality-of-residence registration
- Arrange tax card / Vero matters
- Check Kela eligibility
- Set up bank account and strong authentication
- Arrange housing contract, electricity and home insurance
- Plan public transport / driving
- Apply early for daycare/school if needed
- Register with employment/integration services where relevant
- Use the local newcomer service for initial guidance

...

Source check: 24 August 2026.

...

### Checklist

- Confusing personal identity code with municipality of residence
- Assuming Kela starts automatically
- Delaying tax card
- Assuming bank KYC finishes immediately
- Leaving school/daycare too late
- Missing legalisation/translation of foreign civil-status documents
- Treating local guidance as a Migri/DVV decision-maker
- Choosing housing based only on rent

sources.title: Information about stricter requirements for issuing residence permits - Finnish Government
highlights:
### 1. You have applied for a first residence permit in Finland

According to the Aliens Act, an application for a first residence permit must usually be submitted outside Finland. Once the legislative amendments have entered into force, we will apply a stricter approach to applications for a first residence permit that have been submitted in Finland.

- You can get a negative residence permit decision if you apply for a first residence permit in Finland.
- There are certain situations where you can apply for a first residence permit in Finland, for example if 

- you are a family member of a Finnish citizen
- you apply for a residence permit for a child born in Finland
- you apply for a residence permit for studies or you are a family member of a student
- you apply for a residence permit for a researcher or you are a family member of a researcher
- Each application will be examined individually. When making a decision on your residence permit application, all facts and circumstances affecting your situation will be taken into account. On that basis, we will assess whether it is unreasonable to reject your residence permit application and whether there are obstacles to issuing a residence permit with regard to general obedience to the law, managed migration or internal security.
- As before, the following can be applied for only in Finland: an extended permit, a permanent residence permit, registration of an EU citizen, international protection, temporary protection, a residence permit for a victim of human trafficking, a residence permit due to misconduct of the employer and a residence permit on a discretionary basis on humanitarian grounds.

### 2. You have applied for a residence permit without having a passport issued by your country of nationality

- When you apply for a residence permit, you must usually have a valid passport issued by your country of nationality. If you, for instance, have a refugee travel document or an alien’s passport issued by Finland or some other country, you will not necessarily be able to get a residence permit in Finland.
- For more information, see our customer bulletin: Stricter identification requirements for residence permit applicants

...

## Your own actions will be given more weight when your application is being examined

The following situations, for example, can result in a negative residence permit decision:

- You have given the authorities false information about your identity or nationality or the true purpose of your stay in Finland, for example.
- You have presented forged documents.
- You have resided in Finland illegally. 
- You have knowingly worked in Finland illegally, that is without having the right to work. 
- You have submitted a manifestly unfounded application so that you would not have to leave the country.
- You have tried to mislead the authorities in some other way.

...

Apply for an extended permit or a permanent residence permit before your current residence permit expires. You can get a negative decision if you apply for an extended permit or a permanent residence permit after your previous permit has expired. 

- If you have sent your application in the online service Enter Finland before the expiry of your previous permit, you have applied for a new permit in time.

Citizens ... Everyone else applies to Migri (Finnish Immigration Service; Migrationsverket in Swedish) before coming, because a first permit for work cannot be applied for from inside Finland – see part 2.

Have birth, marriage and divorce certificates and diplomas legalised and translated before you leave: the authorities accept Finnish, Swedish or English, nothing else. Removal goods from outside the EU customs territory need a customs declaration within 12 months of the move, and pets fall under the Finnish Food Authority’s rules, which often require vaccinations.

In Helsinki one address covers most of week one. International House Helsinki, at Ratapihantie 7 in Pasila since 1 June 2026, handles EU registration for Migri, the code and municipality of residence for DVV, the tax card for Vero, jobseeker registration and Kela by remote service, Monday to Friday 9.00–16.00. Identity cards are the exception: newcomers go to the Helsinki Police Department at Pasilanraitio 11. Espoo and Vantaa residents use the same house, because DVV’s Espoo office has closed permanently.

...

If Migri grants you a residence permit, EU registration or a residence card, you are registered automatically and the code comes with the decision. Otherwise you request it from DVV with an online form and visit in person within one month, every family member included; it is free and takes two to three weeks in work and study cases. Tax offices in larger cities issue codes for tax purposes only, usually within one to three business days. Neither of those codes gives you a municipality of residence – for that you still apply to DVV, as part 3 explains.

...

## Three mistakes that cost time or money

| Mistake | What happens | How to avoid it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Assuming the code from Migri or Vero makes you a resident | No kotikunta, so no health station, school place or residence-based benefits | Apply for the municipality of residence at DVV |
| Submitting DVV’s form and forgetting the visit | The visit must take place within one month of the form, for every person | Book the appointment when you submit |
| EU citizen letting three months pass | You are staying without registering and cannot get a kotikunta | Apply to Migri within three months of arrival |

Source: InfoFinland, DVV and Migri, read 24 September 2026.

sources.title: Residence permit and official matters for new students - UEF Kamu
highlights:
Required steps

1. Submit the residence permit application online. Start the application process as early as possible.
2. Visit a Finnish embassy or consulate (opens in a new tab) within 3 months to verify your identity. There may not be a Finnish mission in your country or residence. You may need to travel to another country.

...

#### What is required for the residence permit application?

You will need

- online application (opens in a new tab)
- a valid passport
- health insurance covering medical treatment
- letter of acceptance from UEF
- proof of sufficient funds
- tuition fee or scholarship information (if applicable)

Processing time

- typically 1-3 months, depending on your country
- Do not book flights before your residence permit is granted.
- Late or incomplete applications may cause delays.

...

All students staying over 3 months must have a Finnish personal identity code. You might have it on your residence permit card already.

If you don’t have the Finnish personal identity code, you must visit the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV) (opens in a new tab) in person to

- register as a foreigner (opens in a new tab)
- obtain the Finnish Personal Identity Code (opens in a new tab)
- (if eligible) apply for a municipality of residence (opens in a new tab)
- submit a notification of move (opens in a new tab)

Bring with you

- passport or official ID
- UEF study certificate
- residence permit (if applicable)
- If family members move with you: marriage and children’s birth certificates

After receiving your Finnish personal identity code, inform the UEF Student and Learning Services about it.

You should always use your Finnish personal identity code in all the official matters in Finland. For example when visiting a doctor, opening a bank account, getting your medical prescription, getting a Finnish tax card etc. This code differentiates persons from each other in all Finnish data bases.
